This is KONGSBERG
KONGSBERG protects people and critical infrastructure – from deep sea to space. Through innovation, collaboration and determination, we develop technologies and solutions to serve the defence, security and surveillance markets.
About us
We combine military and civilian expertise to drive rapid innovation for defence, research, and commercial applications.
Our defence and security solutions include strike missiles, remote weapon stations, air defence systems, command and control systems and digital remote towers for customers worldwide. Our solutions help strengthen countries' security and defence capabilities.
KONGSBERG also serves the ocean space with technology – from sensors to autonomous systems – to ensure sustainable management of marine resources, monitor climate change and critical infrastructure, and safeguard national security.
KONGSBERG delivers to every part of the space value chain – from launch services and production of small satellites to downloading and managing satellite data.
The company was founded in 1814 in the town of Kongsberg, Norway. Today, we are more than 7,500 employees in about 20 countries. The company is headquartered in Norway and listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange. The Norwegian government controls about 50.01 percent of the shares in KONGSBERG.
Through innovation and state-of-the-art industrial production, we create jobs and value for our suppliers, partners, customers and owners.
We protect people and planet by innovating technology today, for a better tomorrow.
Three strong divisions
KONGSBERG consists of three divisions:
- Defence Systems
- Missiles & Aerostructures
- Discovery
Defence Systems
This division focuses on land systems, air and coastal defence, naval systems and advanced defence solutions. It includes core defence capabilities such as integrated defence systems, weapon platforms and advanced operational solutions. The division carries significant responsibility for deliveries within highly regulated defence environments and plays a central role in meeting growing demand from NATO and allied markets.
Missiles & Aerostructures
This division brings together missile programmes, aerostructures and maintenance capabilities. It includes both subsonic and supersonic missile programmes, aerostructures production and maintenance of airborne platforms. It also has a dedicated Emerging Business unit to support innovation and new growth areas. The division consolidates advanced manufacturing and programme execution under one structure, strengthening end-to-end accountability across complex value chains.
Discovery
This division integrates the former business area Kongsberg Discovery with Space and Surveillance activities. It combines capabilities in underwater technology, sensors, satellite systems and surveillance, creating a cohesive environment for dual-use and cross-domain innovation. Most civilian-oriented activities are gathered within this division. This allows these businesses to operate with the flexibility required to compete in international civilian markets, without being subject to defence-specific rules and processes that apply elsewhere in the company. At the same time, the division benefits from close collaboration with defence and space activities, strengthening technology development across domains.
Ownership structure
Kongsberg Gruppen ASA is listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange and is subject to Norwegian securities legislation and stock exchange regulations. The Norwegian state owns 50.004 per cent of the shares in the company.
More about the company
Sustainability and corporate social responsibility
Sustainability and corporate social responsibility are important for KONGSBERG and are an integral part of our strategy. We shall conduct our business in a sustainable and accountable manner, and we must carry out our corporate social responsibility in accordance with the applicable expectations of society. This gives KONGSBERG the necessary ‘licence to operate’ in order to execute our business.
The UN has defined 17 sustainability development goals the world should reach by 2030. Several of these goals can only be achieved through innovation and the sensible application of technology. To KONGSBERG, this involves business opportunities in several markets viewed in the light of our broad technology and skills platform.
KONGSBERG has acceded to the UN Global Compact initiative. We support and respect international human and employee rights such as the UN’s Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ILO Core Conventions and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. KONGSBERG uses the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) guidelines for the voluntary reporting of sustainable development.

“KONGSBERG will be better positioned to navigate and grasp opportunities in its markets with a Board of Directors and executive leadership that are solely focused on defence, security and related matters,” said Reiten.

This is why we exist – and why I believe we are positioned to continue to grow.
Eirik Lie, President and Chief Executive Officer of KONGSBERG.

“Together, we combine a unique blend of military and civilian expertise to drive rapid innovation for defence, research, and commercial applications. KONGSBERG delivers to the whole space value chain – from launch services and production of small satellites to downloading and managing satellite data.
KONGSBERG has three strong divisions: Missiles and Aerostructures, Discovery and Defence Systems.

KONGSBERG has a long and proud history.
From its starting point in Norway in 1814, to the international corporation of today, KONGSBERG has been an innovative technology environment.
Through our foresight and ability to adapt, KONGSBERG has survived through changing times and markets, celebrating our 200-year anniversary in 2014, now stronger than ever.
The history of “Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk” dates back to a time before Norway's Constitution was established in 1814. Following the dissolution of the union with Denmark, the need arose to establish a strong defence to ensure Norway's independence and security.
At this time, the silver mines in Kongsberg experienced a decline, but the town already had a significant pool of expertise and established industry through “Jernverket”. It was in this context that Poul Steenstrup, one of the members of the Constitutional Assembly at Eidsvoll, founded "Kongsberg Vaabenfabrik" on March 20, 1814, with approval from Prince Regent Christian Frederik.
Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk started producing rifles for the Norwegian Armed Forces. Increasing deliveries throughout the 19th century lead to the big international breakthrough in 1888, when director Ole Hermann Johannes Krag and gunsmith Erik Jørgensen introduced the prototype of their new rifle.
The rifle was bought by the Danish army in 1889. Three years later, the Krag-Jørgensen became world-famous when the United States decided to equip its soldiers with the rifle.
Krag-Jørgensen was to dominate the production at Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk until the end of the first world war in 1918.
Modern times
In the start of 1918 the company also introduced production for the civil market.
Three years later, the first tools from Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk were launched on the market. These included adjustable spanners, twist drills, chisels, planes, spade handles, blades for circular saws and a range of pliers – to name but a few.
As always, these products were top quality and won the company a gold medal during the International Exposition in Barcelona in 1929.
The company's new production plans for the civil market covered much more than tools however. In the early 1920s, the company launched axle shafts and components for cars and ships, sledges with skis as runners, complete bicycles, dining room furniture, tool cabinets, irons and even a couple of prototypes for sewing machines. Whaling guns became particularly popular for export.
                            
In the 1930s, the threat of war dominated Europe once again and Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk manufactured amongst others antiaircraft guns under license.
During the Second World War, from 1940 to 1945, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was controlled by the Nazi German occupants, whom were unsatisfied with the factory unable to meet expectations due to poor access to raw materials and resistance among factory workers.
Industrial leader
After the end of the Second World War, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was designated as one of key companies in the rebuilding and developing of Norwegian industry and in 1953 the owner, The Norwegian Parliament, initiated a large scale modernization of the company.
This was motivated by the desire to build a national, high tech defence industry that could meet the Norwegian armed forces' needs and contribute to NATO.
The establishment of the Norwegian Armed Forces' research institute at Kjeller in 1947 was part of the strategy. The Norwegian authorities wanted a national industrial partner for the Armed Forces to realise the technology.
From the 1950s to the present, this collaboration has resulted in a number of defence systems such as the Penguin missile, the HUGIN underwater vessel and the Naval Strike Missile.
Innovative breakthroughs
In the 1970s, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was divided into separate divisions as they emerged with specific responsibilities to; maintain aircraft parts, produce automotive parts, develop and produce gas turbines, subsea oil installations, maritime equipment, drawing machines, CNCs and defence equipment.
Dynamic positioning and subsea installations were revolutionary technologies, which gave the city of Kongsberg a technological edge that still prevails today.
New start
The year 1987 was a turning point in the company’s history. Although the level of innovation was high, it was not profitable. The Norwegian state, which owned all the shares, decided to sell all divisions except the defence division which continued under the name Norsk Forsvarsteknologi as.
In 1995 the company reclaim Kongsberg in the new company identity; Kongsberg Gruppen ASA (KONGSBERG). In 1997, KONGSBERG acquired Kongsberg Maritime AS which together with newly established Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace AS (formerly named Kongsberg Gruppen ASA) became two business areas.

Taking scientific echosounders to autonomous platforms
As ocean research moves towards increasingly autonomous operations, integrating proven scientific instruments onto new platforms opens up new possibilities for sustained and efficient ecosystem monitoring.
During a two-week trial in Plymouth, KONGSBERG supported the integration of an EK80 scientific echosounder with two transducers into the National Oceanography Centre’s Autosub Long Range autonomous underwater vehicle, ALR1500, better known as Boaty McBoatface.
The National Oceanography Centre's ALR1500 vessel, aka "Boaty MycBoatface", being lowered into the water. (Photo: Lillian Lieber)
From left - Dr Lilian Lieber, Dr Peter Miller and Dr Yang Yang heading out to see during the two-week trial (Photo: Lillian Lieber)
Members of the trial team at Turnchapel Wharf, which played an instrumental role in making the trial deployments possible (Photo: Dr Yang Yang)
Dr Lilian Lieber and the ALR1500 during the two-week trial off the coast of Plymouth (Photo: Peter Miller)
KONGSBERG Ocean Science Product Advisor Robert Sørhagen joined the team in Plymouth, providing specialist expertise and support throughout the integration and trials. “This trial is a great example of what can be achieved when scientific expertise, autonomous technology and advanced ocean instrumentation come together,” Sørhagen said. “Working closely with the University of Plymouth and the National Oceanography Centre, we are bringing proven scientific echosounder technology to autonomous platforms and enabling new ways to study marine ecosystems.”
                        
This trial is a great example of what can be achieved when scientific expertise, autonomous technology and advanced ocean instrumentation come together
Robert Sørhagen, Product Advisor Ocean Science, KONGSBERG
Combined with other onboard sensors, the EK80 was used to observe fish and zooplankton in the water column alongside measurements of the physical and biogeochemical conditions that influence their distribution. Early observations included a large fish school detected by the EK80, followed by a pod of common dolphins swimming alongside the AUV.
Building a fuller picture of the ocean
The trial forms part of Frontline, a £3.5 million consortium within the UK's NERC ECOFlow programme. The project is exploring how ocean fronts influence marine ecosystems and how these dynamic environments could be affected by the expansion of floating offshore wind in the Celtic Sea.
By combining autonomous platforms with scientific echosounders, satellite observations, and other ocean monitoring technologies, researchers can collect complementary measurements over wider areas and for longer periods. The approach can help build the ecosystem understanding needed as offshore wind developments move into deeper and more complex marine environments.
For KONGSBERG, the collaboration reflects our ambition to support a sustainable ocean by bringing versatile scientific echosounder technology to new platforms and applications. Working closely with our customers at the University of Plymouth and the National Oceanography Centre also supports their transition towards autonomous platforms for future ecosystem assessments.
The trial is an important step towards more extensive scientific surveys planned in the Celtic Sea in 2027. It successfully demonstrates the wider potential of autonomous ocean observation for research in offshore wind regions across Europe and highlights the combination of space-borne and in situ observations to build a fuller picture of dynamic ocean features.
The Frontline collaboration brings together the University of Plymouth, Heriot-Watt University, Plymouth Marine Laboratory, the National Oceanography Centre, SINTEF Ocean, HiDef Aerial Surveying Ltd and KONGSBERG. The Plymouth trial was also supported by Turnchapel Wharf, Zero USV and Thales.
About the Frontline project
Frontline is investigating how floating offshore wind (FLOW) development could affect ocean fronts and marine biodiversity – from plankton to predators – in the Celtic Sea.
The project combines autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) surveys, satellite remote sensing, aerial surveys, seabird tracking, fisheries data and stakeholder engagement to investigate how ocean fronts shape ecological processes and fishing activity across the Celtic Sea, and how these may change with the expansion of large-scale FLOW development.

Belgium is making a major investment in its ground-based air defence capabilities, working closely with its Dutch neighbour. On Monday 9 November, the two countries marked their air defence cooperation at the Royal Military Academy in Brussels, with KONGSBERG's NASAMS playing an important role.
- 
                        
Text:Amanda Chapman-Stavn / KONGSBERG Photo:Amanda Chapman-Stavn / KONGSBERG
The event brought together representatives from Belgium, the Netherlands and the defence industry to mark the next step in Belgium's air defence plans. KONGSBERG attended alongside Rheinmetall Air Defence and Thales Netherlands. The programme also included a symbolic signing ceremony marking the defence cooperation between Belgium and the Netherlands.
                        
We are proud to welcome Belgium to the NASAMS family. With its open architecture and proven flexibility, NASAMS can be tailored to meet evolving operational requirements, and continuously develop and expand its capabilities.
Kjetil Reiten Myhra, EVP KONGSBERG and President Defence Systems.
The ceremony followed the signing of a NOK 10 billion contract in September for the delivery of NASAMS to Belgium, making it the 18th nation to select the system. The Netherlands, already a NASAMS user, is procuring the systems on Belgium's behalf, with the Belgian Air Force as the end user.
With NASAMS on both sides of the border, Belgium and the Netherlands can work more closely on training, share operational experience and coordinate their air defence – strengthening their ability to respond to threats together.
Belgium and the Netherlands already work closely to protect Benelux airspace, including through shared fighter aircraft responsibilities. With NASAMS, they now have the opportunity to extend that cooperation to ground-based air defence.
                            
Building on an established partnership
The Netherlands is already an experienced NASAMS operator and is continuing to expand its own air defence capabilities.
On the same day the Belgian contract was announced, KONGSBERG signed a further NOK 1.5 billion agreement with the Netherlands to expand its CITADEL programme. The contract includes additional NASAMS capabilities and several NOMADS systems, KONGSBERG's highly mobile short-range air defence solution.
                            
The new orders build on KONGSBERG's longstanding relationship with the Netherlands, including the original CITADEL contract signed in 2024.
With both countries investing in NASAMS, the cooperation marked in Brussels supports closer coordination of ground-based air defence in the region, as European allies increasingly look to common capabilities to strengthen their defence capabilities.

Turning defence investment into operational capabilities requires more than technology. At the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo, KONGSBERG highlighted how governments, industry and operational users can work together to deliver solutions for the North Atlantic and High North.
- 
                        
Text:Njål Frilseth / KONGSBERG Photo:NATO
Representatives from 29 countries gathered in Oslo on 11–12 November for the Atlantic Future Forum, hosted aboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales at the invitation of Norway and the United Kingdom. The event featured contributions from more than 50 political, military, government and industry leaders, focusing on international security, technology and industrial partnerships.f
The carrier arrived following its participation in NATO's Arctic Sentry and other allied activities in Norwegian waters. British carrier aircraft had operated alongside Norwegian F-35 fighter jets, while the Norwegian frigate KNM Fridtjof Nansen joined the carrier group, demonstrating practical cooperation between allied forces.
                            
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte emphasised the importance of maritime security for international trade, energy supplies and vital communications.
                            
Describing the North Atlantic as “the bridge that connects the two continents in our Alliance,” he also called on the defence industry to increase production, accelerate innovation and work together to meet growing demand.
For KONGSBERG, closer collaboration between governments and industry is essential to translating defence investments into operational capabilities.
“Agreeing on shared ambitions is important, but what matters is what we deliver together. Involving industry early allows us to combine expertise, develop technology and build the capacity needed to deliver,” said Eirik Lie, President and CEO of KONGSBERG.
Connecting technology and expertise in the High North
Lie participated in a panel discussion on Northern Europe, the High North and Arctic, addressing the challenges of protecting critical underwater infrastructure and the importance of clear responsibilities between authorities, operators and industry.
Camilla Kiss, Executive Vice President and President of Discovery at KONGSBERG, also joined a discussion on securing the North Atlantic and High North at the International Sea Power Conference, held aboard the carrier alongside the forum.
                        
We have the technology and experience to operate in harsh environments, from space to beneath Arctic ice. Now we need governments, users, and industry to work more closely to turn investment into capability at sea.
Camilla Kiss, Executive Vice President and President of Discovery at KONGSBERG
Protecting critical maritime infrastructure requires technologies and organisations to work together. Underwater sensors, autonomous systems, satellite surveillance and secure communications can provide vital information, but effective protection also depends on clear responsibilities and the ability to respond.
Kiss highlighted KONGSBERG's joint High North Proposal with BAE Systems, presented to the relevant Norwegian and British authorities to explore closer cooperation on maritime security and the protection of critical underwater infrastructure.
She also pointed to the EU-funded HiAOOS research project, where KONGSBERG contributes ocean observation technology, supported by the Norwegian Coast Guard, to improve understanding of Arctic conditions.

How can existing technology help society become better prepared for crises? And how can we inspire more children to become the technology creators of tomorrow? These were the challenges facing students in this year's Your Extreme competition. After 48 hours of developing ideas and working together, the winners were announced at award ceremonies in Kongsberg and Trondheim, Norway.
- 
                        
Text:Njål Frilseth / KONGSBERG Photo:Magnus Bjørnnes / KONGSBERG
Every year, KONGSBERG challenges students to think differently, collaborate across disciplines and find creative solutions to societal challenges. Through the student competition Your Extreme, participants have just 48 hours to turn a problem into a concrete proposal for a solution.
The competition was organised in collaboration with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and the University of South-Eastern Norway (USN).
Students could choose between two challenges. The first focused on emergency preparedness and how existing civilian technology could be used in new ways when a serious crisis strikes. The second challenged students to develop solutions that spark children's curiosity about technology and inspire them to become creators themselves.
The result was a wide range of ideas, from alternative payment solutions and navigation without GPS to new ways of teaching children programming.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Kongsberg, CEO Eirik Lie emphasised the importance of challenging established ways of thinking.
                        
Even though we have a great deal of experience at KONGSBERG, that does not mean we have all the answers. Sometimes we simply need fresh perspectives on old challenges. And perhaps you are the ones who will see opportunities the rest of us have overlooked.
Eirik Lie, President & CEO
He also highlighted the need to develop the technological expertise Norway will depend on in the years ahead.
"We must continue to develop new knowledge, challenge established ways of doing things and invest in the people who will create tomorrow's solutions," said Lie.
Learning programming through play wins in Kongsberg
At the award ceremony in Kongsberg, the main prize went to Just Works for their concept, Skift.
The team developed the idea of a wristband that turns programming into a hands-on, playful activity. Using components embedded in the wristband's strap, children can put together code, experiment and learn through trial and error, without having to sit in front of a screen.
The concept is designed to grow with the pupils. Older children can, for example, create new games and challenges for younger pupils.
The jury particularly highlighted how the solution makes programming tangible and accessible while encouraging collaboration and learning across different age groups.
Second place went to Løserne, who explored how existing fibre networks and coastal, radio and mountain stations could provide ships with accurate time and positioning information if GPS systems become unavailable. Through simulation, the team demonstrated how the solution could contribute to safer navigation.
M1-USN took third place with a concept for using existing drones to fight forest fires. The drones could be used to dampen firebreaks, extinguish smaller fires and transport equipment to areas that are difficult to access.
Two special awards were also presented in Kongsberg.
The Innovation Award went to We Have No Idea for Beredskapshylla, a concept that uses electronic shelf labels in grocery stores to communicate important information during emergencies. The displays could show messages from authorities, stock availability and information about upcoming deliveries.
The Sustainability Award went to GER for Nødvaluta 2.0. The team proposed using existing reverse vending machines to issue paper vouchers if digital payment systems become unavailable. These vouchers could be used to purchase essential goods such as food, medicine and fuel.
                            
Trondheim winners aim to teach schoolchildren about emergency preparedness

KONGSBERG has a long and proud history.
From its starting point in Norway in 1814, to the international corporation of today, KONGSBERG has been an innovative technology environment.
Through our foresight and ability to adapt, KONGSBERG has survived through changing times and markets, celebrating our 200-year anniversary in 2014, now stronger than ever.
The history of “Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk” dates back to a time before Norway's Constitution was established in 1814. Following the dissolution of the union with Denmark, the need arose to establish a strong defence to ensure Norway's independence and security.
At this time, the silver mines in Kongsberg experienced a decline, but the town already had a significant pool of expertise and established industry through “Jernverket”. It was in this context that Poul Steenstrup, one of the members of the Constitutional Assembly at Eidsvoll, founded "Kongsberg Vaabenfabrik" on March 20, 1814, with approval from Prince Regent Christian Frederik.
Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk started producing rifles for the Norwegian Armed Forces. Increasing deliveries throughout the 19th century lead to the big international breakthrough in 1888, when director Ole Hermann Johannes Krag and gunsmith Erik Jørgensen introduced the prototype of their new rifle.
The rifle was bought by the Danish army in 1889. Three years later, the Krag-Jørgensen became world-famous when the United States decided to equip its soldiers with the rifle.
Krag-Jørgensen was to dominate the production at Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk until the end of the first world war in 1918.
Modern times
In the start of 1918 the company also introduced production for the civil market.
Three years later, the first tools from Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk were launched on the market. These included adjustable spanners, twist drills, chisels, planes, spade handles, blades for circular saws and a range of pliers – to name but a few.
As always, these products were top quality and won the company a gold medal during the International Exposition in Barcelona in 1929.
The company's new production plans for the civil market covered much more than tools however. In the early 1920s, the company launched axle shafts and components for cars and ships, sledges with skis as runners, complete bicycles, dining room furniture, tool cabinets, irons and even a couple of prototypes for sewing machines. Whaling guns became particularly popular for export.
                            
In the 1930s, the threat of war dominated Europe once again and Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk manufactured amongst others antiaircraft guns under license.
During the Second World War, from 1940 to 1945, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was controlled by the Nazi German occupants, whom were unsatisfied with the factory unable to meet expectations due to poor access to raw materials and resistance among factory workers.
Industrial leader
After the end of the Second World War, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was designated as one of key companies in the rebuilding and developing of Norwegian industry and in 1953 the owner, The Norwegian Parliament, initiated a large scale modernization of the company.
This was motivated by the desire to build a national, high tech defence industry that could meet the Norwegian armed forces' needs and contribute to NATO.
The establishment of the Norwegian Armed Forces' research institute at Kjeller in 1947 was part of the strategy. The Norwegian authorities wanted a national industrial partner for the Armed Forces to realise the technology.
From the 1950s to the present, this collaboration has resulted in a number of defence systems such as the Penguin missile, the HUGIN underwater vessel and the Naval Strike Missile.
Innovative breakthroughs
In the 1970s, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk was divided into separate divisions as they emerged with specific responsibilities to; maintain aircraft parts, produce automotive parts, develop and produce gas turbines, subsea oil installations, maritime equipment, drawing machines, CNCs and defence equipment.
Dynamic positioning and subsea installations were revolutionary technologies, which gave the city of Kongsberg a technological edge that still prevails today.
New start
The year 1987 was a turning point in the company’s history. Although the level of innovation was high, it was not profitable. The Norwegian state, which owned all the shares, decided to sell all divisions except the defence division which continued under the name Norsk Forsvarsteknologi as.

This is KONGSBERG
KONGSBERG protects people and critical infrastructure – from deep sea to space. Through innovation, collaboration and determination, we develop technologies and solutions to serve the defence, security and surveillance markets.
About us
We combine military and civilian expertise to drive rapid innovation for defence, research, and commercial applications.
Our defence and security solutions include strike missiles, remote weapon stations, air defence systems, command and control systems and digital remote towers for customers worldwide. Our solutions help strengthen countries' security and defence capabilities.
KONGSBERG also serves the ocean space with technology – from sensors to autonomous systems – to ensure sustainable management of marine resources, monitor climate change and critical infrastructure, and safeguard national security.
KONGSBERG delivers to every part of the space value chain – from launch services and production of small satellites to downloading and managing satellite data.
The company was founded in 1814 in the town of Kongsberg, Norway. Today, we are more than 7,500 employees in about 20 countries. The company is headquartered in Norway and listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange. The Norwegian government controls about 50.01 percent of the shares in KONGSBERG.
Through innovation and state-of-the-art industrial production, we create jobs and value for our suppliers, partners, customers and owners.
We protect people and planet by innovating technology today, for a better tomorrow.
Three strong divisions
KONGSBERG consists of three divisions:
- Defence Systems
- Missiles & Aerostructures
- Discovery
Defence Systems
This division focuses on land systems, air and coastal defence, naval systems and advanced defence solutions. It includes core defence capabilities such as integrated defence systems, weapon platforms and advanced operational solutions. The division carries significant responsibility for deliveries within highly regulated defence environments and plays a central role in meeting growing demand from NATO and allied markets.
Missiles & Aerostructures
This division brings together missile programmes, aerostructures and maintenance capabilities. It includes both subsonic and supersonic missile programmes, aerostructures production and maintenance of airborne platforms. It also has a dedicated Emerging Business unit to support innovation and new growth areas. The division consolidates advanced manufacturing and programme execution under one structure, strengthening end-to-end accountability across complex value chains.
Discovery
This division integrates the former business area Kongsberg Discovery with Space and Surveillance activities. It combines capabilities in underwater technology, sensors, satellite systems and surveillance, creating a cohesive environment for dual-use and cross-domain innovation. Most civilian-oriented activities are gathered within this division. This allows these businesses to operate with the flexibility required to compete in international civilian markets, without being subject to defence-specific rules and processes that apply elsewhere in the company. At the same time, the division benefits from close collaboration with defence and space activities, strengthening technology development across domains.
Ownership structure
Kongsberg Gruppen ASA is listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange and is subject to Norwegian securities legislation and stock exchange regulations. The Norwegian state owns 50.004 per cent of the shares in the company.
More about the company
Sustainability and corporate social responsibility
Sustainability and corporate social responsibility are important for KONGSBERG and are an integral part of our strategy. We shall conduct our business in a sustainable and accountable manner, and we must carry out our corporate social responsibility in accordance with the applicable expectations of society. This gives KONGSBERG the necessary ‘licence to operate’ in order to execute our business.
The UN has defined 17 sustainability development goals the world should reach by 2030. Several of these goals can only be achieved through innovation and the sensible application of technology. To KONGSBERG, this involves business opportunities in several markets viewed in the light of our broad technology and skills platform.
KONGSBERG has acceded to the UN Global Compact initiative. We support and respect international human and employee rights such as the UN’s Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ILO Core Conventions and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. KONGSBERG uses the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) guidelines for the voluntary reporting of sustainable development.

Following the demerger and separate listing of Kongsberg Maritime, Kongsberg Gruppen ASA (‘KONGSBERG’) is now dedicated to developing the technology and solutions required to protect people and critical infrastructure – from deep sea to space.
“The decision to separate the two companies was taken with an eye on future market opportunities. To create more value in a rapidly changing world, where security and sustainability are expected to dominate in the coming decades,” said Eivind Reiten, Chair of the Board of KONGSBERG Gruppen ASA.
“KONGSBERG will be better positioned to navigate and grasp opportunities in its markets with a Board of Directors and executive leadership that are solely focused on defence, security and related matters,” said Reiten.
                        
I am proud to lead KONGSBERG into the future, together with more than 7,500 highly skilled and motivated colleagues. Our mission – to protect people and planet – has never been more appropriate and right.
This is why we exist – and why I believe we are positioned to continue to grow.
Eirik Lie, President and Chief Executive Officer of KONGSBERG.
Lie succeeds Geir Håøy, who led KONGSBERG as President and CEO from 2016 till 2026.
“Together, we combine a unique blend of military and civilian expertise to drive rapid innovation for defence, research, and commercial applications. Through innovation and state-of-the-art industrial production, we will continue to create jobs and value for our suppliers, partners, customers and owners,” he added.
A focused technology company
KONGSBERG’s defence and security solutions include strike missiles NSM and JSM, PROTECTOR remote weapon stations and Counter-UAS system, the NASAMS air defence system for customers worldwide. The company also serves the ocean space with advanced technology – from sensors to autonomous systems, including the HUGIN autonomous underwater vehicle – to ensure sustainable management of marine resources, monitor climate change and critical infrastructure, and safeguard national security. KONGSBERG delivers to the whole space value chain – from launch services and production of small satellites to downloading and managing satellite data.
KONGSBERG has three strong divisions: Missiles and Aerostructures, Discovery and Defence Systems.
The company was founded in 1814 in the town of Kongsberg, Norway. Today, KONGSBERG has more than 7,500 employees in about 20 countries. The company is headquartered in Norway and listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange.

Shape the future with us
Join KONGSBERG and be part of a leading technology company developing advanced solutions for defence, security, oceans, space and critical infrastructure. Across our organisation, we combine deep domain expertise with innovation and collaboration to create technology that protects people, supports society and strengthens national capabilities.
Explore our vision and uncover your career potential
Our people are at the centre of everything we do. Bringing together diverse skills, perspectives and experience, we work across disciplines to solve complex challenges and deliver high-performance solutions in demanding environments. This is where technology, purpose and teamwork come together.
At KONGSBERG, you will have the opportunity to work on meaningful projects with real-world impact, from next-generation defence systems and underwater technology to space and digital solutions. Explore your opportunities and build your future with KONGSBERG.
Do you have questions about applying for a job with us? Find the answers here.

- We offer a diverse range of roles across various disciplines, reflecting its commitment to innovation and excellence.. Opportunities are available in areas such as systems engineering, project management, mechanical and electrical engineering, software development, and more.
- We support professional growth and development through a variety of initiatives that foster continuous learning, skill enhancement, and career progression. We ensure that employees have ample opportunities to grow in their careers while staying at the forefront of technological and industry advancements.
- KONGSBERG is deeply committed to sustainability, integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles into its core operations. This commitment is reflected in several key areas of our business.

- Our onboarding process is designed to provide new hires with a seamless and efficient transition into their roles. We equip them with the necessary tools, resources, and information to succeed from day one. In addition to professional development, we place a strong emphasis on fostering a sense of belonging and community, ensuring that our employees feel valued and connected within the organization.
- Your application should include an updated CV/resume and a cover letter explaining why you’re interested in the position and how your skills and experiences make you a great fit. Make sure to tailor your application to the specific role you’re applying for.
- We offer a comprehensive benefits package, including competitive salaries, health and wellness programs, flexible work arrangements, opportunities for international assignments, and more. Specific benefits may vary by location and role.

KONGSBERG has a long and proud history.
From its starting point in Norway in 1814, to the international corporation of today, KONGSBERG has been an innovative technology environment.
Through our foresight and ability to adapt, KONGSBERG has survived through changing times and markets, celebrating our 200-year anniversary in 2014, now stronger than ever.

A recent marine autonomy trial off the coast of Plymouth brought together new observing capabilities, including KONGSBERG scientific echosounder technology and a miniaturized holographic plankton imaging sensor from the University of Plymouth aboard the National Oceanography Centre’s Autosub Long Range AUV Boaty McBoatface to study marine ecosystems at oceanographic fronts - dynamic boundaries between different water masses important for marine life.
- 
                        
Text:KONGSBERG Photo:Peter Miller
Taking scientific echosounders to autonomous platforms
As ocean research moves towards increasingly autonomous operations, integrating proven scientific instruments onto new platforms opens up new possibilities for sustained and efficient ecosystem monitoring.
During a two-week trial in Plymouth, KONGSBERG supported the integration of an EK80 scientific echosounder with two transducers into the National Oceanography Centre’s Autosub Long Range autonomous underwater vehicle, ALR1500, better known as Boaty McBoatface.
The National Oceanography Centre's ALR1500 vessel, aka "Boaty MycBoatface", being lowered into the water. (Photo: Lillian Lieber)
From left - Dr Lilian Lieber, Dr Peter Miller and Dr Yang Yang heading out to see during the two-week trial (Photo: Lillian Lieber)
Members of the trial team at Turnchapel Wharf, which played an instrumental role in making the trial deployments possible (Photo: Dr Yang Yang)
Dr Lilian Lieber and the ALR1500 during the two-week trial off the coast of Plymouth (Photo: Peter Miller)
KONGSBERG Ocean Science Product Advisor Robert Sørhagen joined the team in Plymouth, providing specialist expertise and support throughout the integration and trials. “This trial is a great example of what can be achieved when scientific expertise, autonomous technology and advanced ocean instrumentation come together,” Sørhagen said. “Working closely with the University of Plymouth and the National Oceanography Centre, we are bringing proven scientific echosounder technology to autonomous platforms and enabling new ways to study marine ecosystems.”
                        
This trial is a great example of what can be achieved when scientific expertise, autonomous technology and advanced ocean instrumentation come together
Robert Sørhagen, Product Advisor Ocean Science, KONGSBERG
Combined with other onboard sensors, the EK80 was used to observe fish and zooplankton in the water column alongside measurements of the physical and biogeochemical conditions that influence their distribution. Early observations included a large fish school detected by the EK80, followed by a pod of common dolphins swimming alongside the AUV.
Building a fuller picture of the ocean
The trial forms part of Frontline, a £3.5 million consortium within the UK's NERC ECOFlow programme. The project is exploring how ocean fronts influence marine ecosystems and how these dynamic environments could be affected by the expansion of floating offshore wind in the Celtic Sea.
By combining autonomous platforms with scientific echosounders, satellite observations, and other ocean monitoring technologies, researchers can collect complementary measurements over wider areas and for longer periods. The approach can help build the ecosystem understanding needed as offshore wind developments move into deeper and more complex marine environments.
For KONGSBERG, the collaboration reflects our ambition to support a sustainable ocean by bringing versatile scientific echosounder technology to new platforms and applications. Working closely with our customers at the University of Plymouth and the National Oceanography Centre also supports their transition towards autonomous platforms for future ecosystem assessments.
The trial is an important step towards more extensive scientific surveys planned in the Celtic Sea in 2027. It successfully demonstrates the wider potential of autonomous ocean observation for research in offshore wind regions across Europe and highlights the combination of space-borne and in situ observations to build a fuller picture of dynamic ocean features.
The Frontline collaboration brings together the University of Plymouth, Heriot-Watt University, Plymouth Marine Laboratory, the National Oceanography Centre, SINTEF Ocean, HiDef Aerial Surveying Ltd and KONGSBERG. The Plymouth trial was also supported by Turnchapel Wharf, Zero USV and Thales.

Frontline is investigating how floating offshore wind (FLOW) development could affect ocean fronts and marine biodiversity – from plankton to predators – in the Celtic Sea.
The project combines autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) surveys, satellite remote sensing, aerial surveys, seabird tracking, fisheries data and stakeholder engagement to investigate how ocean fronts shape ecological processes and fishing activity across the Celtic Sea, and how these may change with the expansion of large-scale FLOW development.

Belgium is making a major investment in its ground-based air defence capabilities, working closely with its Dutch neighbour. On Monday 9 November, the two countries marked their air defence cooperation at the Royal Military Academy in Brussels, with KONGSBERG's NASAMS playing an important role.
- 
                        
Text:Amanda Chapman-Stavn / KONGSBERG Photo:Amanda Chapman-Stavn / KONGSBERG
The event brought together representatives from Belgium, the Netherlands and the defence industry to mark the next step in Belgium's air defence plans. KONGSBERG attended alongside Rheinmetall Air Defence and Thales Netherlands. The programme also included a symbolic signing ceremony marking the defence cooperation between Belgium and the Netherlands.
                        
We are proud to welcome Belgium to the NASAMS family. With its open architecture and proven flexibility, NASAMS can be tailored to meet evolving operational requirements, and continuously develop and expand its capabilities.
Kjetil Reiten Myhra, EVP KONGSBERG and President Defence Systems.
The ceremony followed the signing of a NOK 10 billion contract in September for the delivery of NASAMS to Belgium, making it the 18th nation to select the system. The Netherlands, already a NASAMS user, is procuring the systems on Belgium's behalf, with the Belgian Air Force as the end user.
With NASAMS on both sides of the border, Belgium and the Netherlands can work more closely on training, share operational experience and coordinate their air defence – strengthening their ability to respond to threats together.
Belgium and the Netherlands already work closely to protect Benelux airspace, including through shared fighter aircraft responsibilities. With NASAMS, they now have the opportunity to extend that cooperation to ground-based air defence.
                            
Building on an established partnership
The Netherlands is already an experienced NASAMS operator and is continuing to expand its own air defence capabilities.
On the same day the Belgian contract was announced, KONGSBERG signed a further NOK 1.5 billion agreement with the Netherlands to expand its CITADEL programme. The contract includes additional NASAMS capabilities and several NOMADS systems, KONGSBERG's highly mobile short-range air defence solution.
                            
The new orders build on KONGSBERG's longstanding relationship with the Netherlands, including the original CITADEL contract signed in 2024.
With both countries investing in NASAMS, the cooperation marked in Brussels supports closer coordination of ground-based air defence in the region, as European allies increasingly look to common capabilities to strengthen their defence capabilities.

Text:Njål Frilseth / KONGSBERG Photo:NATO
Representatives from 29 countries gathered in Oslo on 11–12 November for the Atlantic Future Forum, hosted aboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales at the invitation of Norway and the United Kingdom. The carrier arrived following its participation in NATO's Arctic Sentry and other allied activities in Norwegian waters. British carrier aircraft had operated alongside Norwegian F-35 fighter jets, while the Norwegian frigate KNM Fridtjof Nansen joined the carrier group, demonstrating practical cooperation between allied forces.
                            
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte emphasised the importance of maritime security for international trade, energy supplies and vital communications.
                            
Describing the North Atlantic as “the bridge that connects the two continents in our Alliance,” he also called on the defence industry to increase production, accelerate innovation and work together to meet growing demand.
For KONGSBERG, closer collaboration between governments and industry is essential to translating defence investments into operational capabilities.

Connecting technology and expertise in the High North
Lie participated in a panel discussion on Northern Europe, the High North and Arctic, addressing the challenges of protecting critical underwater infrastructure and the importance of clear responsibilities between authorities, operators and industry.
Camilla Kiss, Executive Vice President and President of Discovery at KONGSBERG, also joined a discussion on securing the North Atlantic and High North at the International Sea Power Conference, held aboard the carrier alongside the forum.

Underwater sensors, autonomous systems, satellite surveillance and secure communications can provide vital information, but effective protection also depends on clear responsibilities and the ability to respond.

How can existing technology help society become better prepared for crises? And how can we inspire more children to become the technology creators of tomorrow? These were the challenges facing students in this year's Your Extreme competition. After 48 hours of developing ideas and working together, the winners were announced at award ceremonies in Kongsberg and Trondheim, Norway.
- 
                        
Text:Njål Frilseth / KONGSBERG Photo:Magnus Bjørnnes / KONGSBERG
Every year, KONGSBERG challenges students to think differently, collaborate across disciplines and find creative solutions to societal challenges. Through the student competition Your Extreme, participants have just 48 hours to turn a problem into a concrete proposal for a solution.
The competition was organised in collaboration with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and the University of South-Eastern Norway (USN).
Students could choose between two challenges. The first focused on emergency preparedness and how existing civilian technology could be used in new ways when a serious crisis strikes. The second challenged students to develop solutions that spark children's curiosity about technology and inspire them to become creators themselves.
The result was a wide range of ideas, from alternative payment solutions and navigation without GPS to new ways of teaching children programming.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Kongsberg, CEO Eirik Lie emphasised the importance of challenging established ways of thinking.
                        
Even though we have a great deal of experience at KONGSBERG, that does not mean we have all the answers. Sometimes we simply need fresh perspectives on old challenges. And perhaps you are the ones who will see opportunities the rest of us have overlooked.
Eirik Lie, President & CEO
He also highlighted the need to develop the technological expertise Norway will depend on in the years ahead.
"We must continue to develop new knowledge, challenge established ways of doing things and invest in the people who will create tomorrow's solutions," said Lie.
Learning programming through play wins in Kongsberg
At the award ceremony in Kongsberg, the main prize went to Just Works for their concept, Skift.
The team developed the idea of a wristband that turns programming into a hands-on, playful activity. Using components embedded in the wristband's strap, children can put together code, experiment and learn through trial and error, without having to sit in front of a screen.
The concept is designed to grow with the pupils. Older children can, for example, create new games and challenges for younger pupils.
The jury particularly highlighted how the solution makes programming tangible and accessible while encouraging collaboration and learning across different age groups.
Second place went to Løserne, who explored how existing fibre networks and coastal, radio and mountain stations could provide ships with accurate time and positioning information if GPS systems become unavailable. Through simulation, the team demonstrated how the solution could contribute to safer navigation.
M1-USN took third place with a concept for using existing drones to fight forest fires. The drones could be used to dampen firebreaks, extinguish smaller fires and transport equipment to areas that are difficult to access.
Two special awards were also presented in Kongsberg.
The Innovation Award went to We Have No Idea for Beredskapshylla, a concept that uses electronic shelf labels in grocery stores to communicate important information during emergencies. The displays could show messages from authorities, stock availability and information about upcoming deliveries.
The Sustainability Award went to GER for Nødvaluta 2.0. The team proposed using existing reverse vending machines to issue paper vouchers if digital payment systems become unavailable. These vouchers could be used to purchase essential goods such as food, medicine and fuel.
                            
Trondheim winners aim to teach schoolchildren about emergency preparedness
In Trondheim, the main prize went to Claude-effort Ultra-max "Make no mistakes", who developed the concept Strømbrudd (Power Outage).
The idea is a hands-on technology day for seventh-grade pupils, during which they experience a simulated power outage and must work together to restore essential societal functions.
                            
Through ten practical challenges, pupils explore topics including electricity supply, energy storage, water supply, communications and digital systems.
The aim is to make technology understandable and relevant through practical experience. The concept is also designed to be delivered in schools without the need for a dedicated laboratory or specialist expertise.
